narrative_idea_gen: **"Die Hard at the World's Fair"** — A breathless parody of *Die Hard* structured as a prestige pseudo-documentary about Alexander Graham Bell, depicting the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial Exposition exclusively as a workplace where every character—janitors, booth operators, security guards, food vendors—is defined solely by their exhibition-floor duties and petty professional grievances. When a monomaniacal Western Union operative seizes the main exhibition hall to destroy Bell's telephone prototype and preserve the telegraph monopoly, Bell becomes an unlikely action hero improvising weapons from Edison's displays and crawling through pneumatic tube networks, while the omniscient narration pulls wide to show how each worker across the fairgrounds experiences the siege purely through the disruption of their specific job. The journey through the sprawling, labyrinthine exposition grounds escalates into increasingly absurd set pieces—a chase through the Machinery Hall involving a runaway Corliss steam engine, a fistfight atop the outstretched torch of the not-yet-assembled Statue of Liberty—but the parody's sharpest knife twists at the end: Bell saves the fair, the telephone works, and he can never go back to being the eccentric nobody he was that morning, stranded permanently in a new world of patent wars, celebrity, and corporate ruthlessness that makes the hostage crisis look quaint.

# Seven Scene-Level Beats for *Die Hard at the World's Fair*

---

## Beat 1: The Exposition as Ecosystem — A Workplace Before It Becomes a Battlefield

**Concrete Action To Write:** Open not with Bell, not with the villain, not with any hint of the siege to come — but with the **fair itself waking up on the morning of the event**, rendered as a pseudo-documentary survey of labor. The omniscient narration introduces the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial Exposition the way a prestige documentary introduces an aircraft carrier or a restaurant kitchen: as a self-contained world defined entirely by job titles and jurisdictional grievances. A janitor in Machinery Hall has a turf dispute with a janitor from Agricultural Hall over who sweeps the connecting vestibule. A food vendor selling George Washington cream puffs near the Main Building resents the oyster stand's superior foot traffic. A security guard has memorized which exhibitors sneak in whiskey. The Corliss steam engine — the fair's technological centerpiece, a seventy-foot behemoth that powers the entire Machinery Hall — requires a dedicated crew who consider themselves the aristocracy of the grounds. Into this ecosystem, almost parenthetically, we drop **Alexander Graham Bell**: a gangly, mutton-chopped nobody with a tiny booth in a bad location, an invention no one has come to see, and a demonstrable inability to navigate the fair's social hierarchies. He can't get the janitor to sweep near his booth. He can't get a cream puff because the line is too long and he's too polite to cut. He is, in workplace terms, the lowest-status employee on the floor.

**Narrative Technique — Worldbuilding as Comic Characterization; The Workplace as Closed System:** The structural function of this opening is identical to the narrator's preamble in *Cathedral*: it teaches the reader **how to read the story**. By opening with the fair-as-workplace rather than the fair-as-historical-event, you establish the governing comedic lens — every character, every crisis, every moment of heroism will be filtered through the language and logic of professional obligation. This is the story's central comedic conceit and it must be planted before a single shot is fired. The pseudo-documentary omniscience is critical: a *Die Hard* parody needs an intimate, ground-level perspective for Bell (the John McClane figure), but the workplace satire needs a wide, Altman-esque eye that can cut across the entire fairgrounds to show how the siege ripples through dozens of micro-jobs. Establishing the **dual register** — tight with Bell, wide with the workforce — in the opening beat means the reader accepts both modes before the plot demands them. Bell's low status is also load-bearing: in *Die Hard*, McClane works because he's an ordinary man in an extraordinary situation. Here, Bell must be **less** than ordinary — actively marginal, a man whose invention is being ignored, whose booth is in the back, who doesn't even register as important enough to resent. This makes his later transformation into an action hero both funnier and, in the story's final turn, more tragic.

**What Must Make It Memorable:** The reader should finish this beat with two feelings held simultaneously: delight at the specificity and absurdity of the workplace ecosystem, and an almost subliminal awareness that we are watching something fragile. This little world — petty, hierarchical, alive with small grievances — is about to be shattered. The detailed ordinariness of the morning IS the stakes. Also: the Corliss engine, the pneumatic tube network, the not-yet-assembled Statue of Liberty torch on display, and Edison's various exhibits must all be introduced here as **workplace infrastructure**, not as Chekhov's guns. The reader should absorb them as set dressing. They'll all come back as weapons or set pieces, but the setup must feel like documentary texture, not foreshadowing.

---

## Beat 2: The Villain's Grievance — Telegraph Infrastructure as Dying Empire

**Concrete Action To Write:** Before the siege begins, pull the omniscient lens toward **Elisha Graves Whitfield** (or whatever the Western Union operative is named) — and deliver his backstory the way a prestige documentary delivers the backstory of a corporate whistleblower or a disgraced executive: with apparent sympathy and meticulous professional detail. Whitfield is a monomaniacal Western Union field superintendent who has spent twenty years building the telegraph network — stringing wire across prairies, through blizzards, over the Rockies. He speaks of telegraph infrastructure the way a medieval monk speaks of cathedral construction: as civilizational destiny. He has a crew of telegraph operators and linemen loyal to him personally, men who share his conviction that the telephone is not merely a competing product but an **ontological threat** — a toy that will unravel a system they built with their hands. Whitfield has been at the fair for weeks. He has watched Bell's little booth with its pathetic foot traffic. He has done the math: if Bell demonstrates the telephone successfully to the judges today, the patents will hold, investment will follow, and everything Whitfield built will begin to die. His plan is simple, professional, and — in his mind — rational: seize the Main Exhibition Building, lock down the hall, destroy the prototype and Bell's documentation, and make it look like the act of a deranged individual rather than an industrial operation. He has timed it for the afternoon judging session, when the Emperor of Brazil, Dom Pedro II, is scheduled to visit Bell's booth. Cut off the demonstration, and the telephone dies in its crib.

**Narrative Technique — Sympathetic Villain Through Professional Specificity; Backstory as Mirror:** This beat does double duty. On the surface, it's the *Die Hard* structural requirement: meet Hans Gruber, understand the heist plan, establish the ticking clock. But the deeper function is **thematic mirroring**. Whitfield is Bell's inverse — a man who DID build something, who DID achieve mastery, who DID earn his place in the professional hierarchy, and who is now watching a younger, stranger, less credentialed man threaten to make his life's work obsolete. The pseudo-documentary voice should treat Whitfield's grievance with the same meticulous respect it gave the janitors and food vendors in Beat 1, because **in the story's workplace logic, Whitfield's complaint is legitimate**. He IS the senior employee being disrupted by the new hire. The comedy comes from the scale of his response; the tragedy comes from the fact that he's *right* — the telephone will destroy the telegraph, and no amount of hostage-taking can change that. The backstory must be delivered in the flat, informational register of a documentary B-roll segment — the prestige narrator explaining telegraph infrastructure with maps and statistics — while the emotional subtext (a man watching his world end) hums underneath. This is the same technique as Carver burying the wife's suicide attempt in the narrator's preamble: catastrophic emotional content delivered in a register that refuses to acknowledge its own weight.

**What Must Make It Memorable:** Whitfield must be *compelling*, not cartoonish. The parody's sharpest edge depends on the villain being someone whose professional pride is recognizable and whose obsolescence is genuinely poignant. If the reader can feel, even for a moment, that Whitfield has a point — that something real is being lost, that the telegraph WAS a miracle, that the men who built it deserve better than to be discarded — then the story's final turn (Bell winning and discovering that victory tastes like corporate ruthlessness) will cut deeper. The villain's grief and the hero's eventual disillusionment are the same grief: the recognition that progress doesn't care about the people who make it.

---

## Beat 3: The Seizure — "I Am Declaring This Exhibition Hall a Closed Circuit"

**Concrete Action To Write:** The siege begins during the peak afternoon hours. Whitfield's men — telegraph operators and linemen, physically tough from years of outdoor infrastructure work — move with coordinated efficiency. They seal the Main Exhibition Building's doors, cut the external telegraph lines (ironic — they know exactly which wires to cut), and take control of the building's internal communication systems. Whitfield makes his announcement to the trapped exhibitors and visitors using a telegraph sounder amplified through a speaking trumpet, deliberately choosing telegraph technology over voice. His demand is procedural, not theatrical: clear the hall, surrender Bell's prototype and patent documentation, and everyone goes home. He frames it as a **regulatory action** — Western Union reclaiming intellectual property it has a right to, a corporate operation that these people are unfortunately caught inside of. The fairgoers and exhibitors are herded into the center of the Main Building. Dom Pedro II is among the hostages, though Whitfield treats him as a scheduling inconvenience more than a political asset. The security guards are neutralized quickly — they were never equipped for anything more serious than catching pickpockets. The omniscient narration pulls wide: across the fairgrounds, every worker experiences the lockdown as a **job-specific disruption**. The food vendors can't get into the Main Building to restock. The janitors' cleaning schedule is ruined. The Machinery Hall crew wonders if they should shut down the Corliss engine. And Alexander Graham Bell, who was in the restroom when the seizure began, finds himself locked OUTSIDE the sealed hall — separated from his prototype, his notes, and his entire reason for being at the fair.

**Narrative Technique — The Inciting Event as Workplace Disruption; The Hero Excluded from His Own Crisis:** The structural pivot here is lifting verbatim from *Die Hard*: the hero is separated from the main hostage group by accident, giving him freedom of movement the villains don't know about. But the comedic and thematic adaptation is crucial — Bell is locked out, not because he was doing something heroic or clever, but because he was **using the restroom**, which is the most unheroic possible reason and also the most workplace-authentic. The omniscient pull-wide to the workforce's reaction is where the pseudo-documentary conceit earns its keep: each worker's response to the crisis is mediated entirely through their job. The cream puff vendor doesn't think "we're all going to die"; he thinks "my inventory is locked in there and the cream is going to turn." The janitor doesn't think "hostages"; he thinks "they're going to track mud everywhere and I'll be the one cleaning it." This is the story's **Comic Rashomon** — the same event experienced through a dozen incompatible professional lenses — and it must be established HERE so it can be deployed throughout the escalation. Meanwhile, Whitfield's choice to use telegraph technology for his announcement is a character detail masquerading as a set piece: he is so committed to his dying medium that he uses it even when a speaking voice would be more efficient. He is performing telegraphic supremacy even as he fights to preserve it.

**What Must Make It Memorable:** The seizure should feel both genuinely tense and absurdly bureaucratic. Whitfield's men are competent and dangerous, but they move like infrastructure professionals executing a work order, not like terrorists. The comedy is in the dissonance between the scale of the act (armed takeover, international hostages, imperial dignitaries) and the language used to describe it (regulatory action, procedural compliance, equipment retrieval). Bell's exclusion from the building is the structural engine for everything that follows, but it also lands as a devastating workplace joke: even in a crisis, Bell is so marginal that the villains don't know he exists. The man whose invention will change the world is, at this moment, standing outside a locked door with no shoes on (he left them at his booth — an homage to McClane's bare feet that also works as period-appropriate eccentricity).

---

## Beat 4: Bell Enters the Infrastructure — Crawling Through the Guts of the Fair

**Concrete Action To Write:** Bell, locked outside the Main Building, must get back inside. He discovers — through knowledge gained from weeks of being ignored near his low-status booth — that the fairground's **pneumatic tube network** connects the buildings underground. These tubes, designed to shuttle messages and small packages between exhibition halls, are just large enough for a lean, desperate man to crawl through. Bell enters the system through a maintenance hatch near Agricultural Hall, guided inadvertently by a janitor who knows the tunnel layout because it's technically his jurisdiction ("I'm not saying to go in there, I'm saying it's *my* section and I know where it goes"). Inside the tubes, Bell encounters the fair's hidden anatomy — the ventilation systems, the gas-line infrastructure, the rat-runs and service corridors that make the gleaming exhibition halls possible. He emerges inside Machinery Hall, adjacent to the Main Building, and begins to improvise his counterattack. He passes through Edison's exhibit — the great man himself is not present, having sent his displays with assistants — and begins cannibalizing the equipment on display. Bell is, for the first time, in his element: among machines, among electrical components, with a problem that requires improvisation. He rigs a crude communication device from Edison's equipment — not a telephone, but a listening apparatus that lets him hear into the Main Building. He hears Whitfield's men coordinating. He hears his wife's (or associate's) voice among the hostages. He begins to plan.

**Narrative Technique — Removal of All Social Mediators; The Hero Alone in the Machine:** This beat maps onto the *Cathedral* structural pivot of the wife falling asleep: the removal of every social buffer that has allowed the protagonist to remain passive. Bell, alone in the pneumatic tubes, is stripped of every role except his essential self. He's not "the exhibitor with the bad booth location" or "the man nobody came to see." He's a man with mechanical knowledge in a mechanical space, and for the first time, his skills are not being judged by a marketplace — they're being demanded by a crisis. The pseudo-documentary narration should shift here: as Bell enters the infrastructure, the camera (as it were) goes with him, and the wide Altman-esque cuts to the workforce continue but grow more urgent, more fragmented. **The dual register tightens.** The cannibalizing of Edison's exhibits is both a *Die Hard* trope (improvised weapons from available materials) and a historical in-joke — Bell literally disassembling his rival's displays to build tools. The listening device is a thematic echo: Bell, the man who has been trying to convince people to *listen* to his invention, now uses a jury-rigged version of that same principle to eavesdrop on his enemy. The tool he couldn't sell becomes the tool that saves him.

**What Must Make It Memorable:** The pneumatic tube crawl is the story's first major set piece and must balance genuine claustrophobic tension with documentary absurdism. Bell should be narrating to himself — muttering, calculating, treating the crisis like a technical problem — and the omniscient voice should be annotating his monologue with historical footnotes and engineering specifications, because **the pseudo-documentary never breaks character**. Even in an action sequence, the narration maintains its calm, informational register, which creates a constant comedic friction with the action on screen/page. The janitor who guides Bell to the tunnel entrance should do so while complaining about how the pneumatic system's maintenance schedule has been neglected — even his act of help is a professional grievance.

---

## Beat 5: Escalation Across the Fairgrounds — Set Pieces as Workplace Catastrophes

**Concrete Action To Write:** This is the story's long second act — a series of escalating confrontations as Bell works his way through the interconnected exhibition buildings toward the Main Hall, engaging Whitfield's men while the omniscient narration tracks the cascading disruption across the entire fair. **Three major set pieces:**

**(A) The Machinery Hall Chase — The Corliss Engine.** Bell is spotted by Whitfield's men in Machinery Hall. The chase triggers a catastrophic accident: someone (Bell, a villain, a panicking bystander) disengages a safety governor on the Corliss steam engine. narrative_story:
# Die Hard at the World's Fair

---

## I.

At 5:47 on the morning of June 25, 1876, the first person to enter the grounds of the Philadelphia Centennial Exposition was not a dignitary, an inventor, a journalist, or a paying guest. It was Herbert Calloway, sixty-one years old, night-shift supervisor of sanitation for Machinery Hall, who had technically never left.

Calloway had been on the grounds since eleven o'clock the previous evening, overseeing the mopping of the twelve-hundred-foot nave, a task that required four men, nine mop-heads (the Exposition Commission authorized six, but Calloway supplemented from personal stock), and a precise choreography that moved east-to-west so that the final stretch of floor dried nearest the sunrise doors. It was, by Calloway's private estimation, the most complex janitorial operation on the continent. He had said this aloud, to no one in particular, on fourteen documented occasions.

The problem — and there was always a problem, because the Centennial Exposition was not, as the newspapers insisted on calling it, a celebration of American ingenuity, but rather a two-hundred-and-thirty-six-acre jurisdictional dispute with bunting — the problem was the vestibule.

The vestibule connecting Machinery Hall to the Main Exhibition Building belonged, depending on which memorandum you consulted, to either Calloway's domain or to the domain of one Franklin Pettit, day-shift supervisor of sanitation for the Main Building. The Exposition Commission's original floor plan placed the vestibule within Machinery Hall's footprint. A revised plan, issued three weeks before opening day, extended the Main Building's boundaries to include it. Neither plan had been formally rescinded. Both were, in the technical parlance of facilities management, "operative." The result was that the vestibule was either cleaned twice daily — Calloway's men at night, Pettit's men in the morning — or not at all, depending on whether the two supervisors were speaking to each other.

They were not, at present, speaking to each other. They had not spoken since the Incident of June 11, when Pettit's assistant had moved Calloway's supply bucket six inches to the left, into what was arguably — *arguably* — Main Building territory, and Calloway had responded by filing a formal complaint with the Commission's Office of Grounds Maintenance, a body that met on alternate Tuesdays and had a backlog of grievances extending to September.

The vestibule, consequently, had not been swept in two weeks. It was becoming an embarrassment. Foreign dignitaries walked through it. The Emperor of Brazil was scheduled to walk through it this very afternoon.

Calloway did not care about the Emperor of Brazil. Calloway cared about the vestibule.

This distinction — between the people who walked through the Centennial Exposition and the people who kept the Centennial Exposition walkable — was the fundamental organizing principle of the grounds, more rigid than any displayed taxonomy of minerals or manufactures. There were visitors and there were workers, and among the workers there was a hierarchy as intricate and fiercely defended as anything the Centennial's anthropological exhibits attributed to the Sandwich Islanders.

At the top: the Corliss crew.

The Corliss Double Walking-Beam Steam Engine stood at the center of Machinery Hall like a cast-iron cathedral. Seventy feet tall. Fourteen hundred horsepower. Two walking beams, each thirty-six feet long. A flywheel thirty feet in diameter and weighing fifty-six tons. It powered every operational machine in the hall — the looms, the lathes, the presses, the saws — through a system of underground shafts and belts that ran beneath the floor like a mechanical circulatory system. The engine required a crew of six: a chief engineer named Hoskins, two firemen, two oilers, and an assistant engineer who also served, in practice, as Hoskins's personal valet, fetching his coffee and buffing his shoes. The Corliss crew existed in a state of professional exaltation that the other workers found simultaneously admirable and intolerable. They wore matching overalls. They had a designated lunch area roped off with velvet cord that Hoskins had requisitioned from the fine-arts pavilion. When President Grant and Dom Pedro II had jointly started the engine on Opening Day — each man grasping one of the two operating levers — Hoskins had been photographed standing between them, and the photograph now hung, framed, above the engine's control platform.

The Corliss crew did not sweep. The Corliss crew did not stock concession supplies or manage ticket queues or patrol for pickpockets. The Corliss crew maintained the heart, and the heart made everything else possible, and if you didn't understand that, then you didn't understand anything, and Hoskins would be happy to explain it to you at length, during working hours, while his assistant fetched another coffee.

Below the Corliss crew, in rough descending order: the security guards (armed with billy clubs and an exaggerated sense of mandate), the telegraph operators (who controlled the grounds' internal communication network and behaved as though this made them spymasters), the exhibit technicians (who maintained the displays and harbored artistic pretensions), the food vendors (who had the only jobs that generated direct cash revenue and resented being near the bottom of the hierarchy despite this), and, finally, the exhibitors themselves — the inventors and manufacturers who had rented booth space to display their wares.

Among the exhibitors, the hierarchy was determined by three factors: booth size, booth location, and foot traffic. A large booth near the Main Building's central transept with a constant crowd was aristocracy. A medium booth along the east nave with respectable traffic was gentry. A small booth in a back corner near the restrooms, with a hand-lettered sign reading "PROFESSOR A. G. BELL — TELEPHONIC DEVICE — ELECTRICAL TRANSMISSION OF VOCAL SOUNDS," and with foot traffic that could be accurately described as "the people who got lost trying to find the restrooms" — that was something below gentry. That was something the hierarchy didn't have a name for, because naming it would have required acknowledging it, and no one had found reason to do so.

Alexander Graham Bell arrived at his booth at 8:15 that morning, which was fifteen minutes after the doors opened and forty-five minutes after the food vendors had begun selling, which meant that the line for Washington cream puffs at the American Bakery Company stand near the entrance was already eighteen people deep. Bell saw the line. Bell wanted a cream puff. Bell was a twenty-nine-year-old Scotsman with muttonchop whiskers that gave him a look of benign befuddlement, as though he had been interrupted mid-thought and never quite recovered, and he was constitutionally incapable of cutting in line. He had once waited forty minutes for a streetcar he could see was already full. He now stood at the back of the cream-puff line for six minutes, shifting his weight, consulting his pocket watch, and performing the internal calculation of a man who has somewhere important to be but who has been raised to believe that asserting this is a form of violence.

He left the line without a cream puff. He would try again later. He told himself this without conviction.

At his booth, the morning was already a small disaster. The exhibit card hanging from the railing — his sole piece of official signage — had curled in the humidity. The wire connecting his transmitter to the receiver, which he had carefully draped across the booth's partition, had been knocked to the floor overnight, probably by a janitor. This was in fact true: one of Calloway's night-shift men had snagged it with a mop handle at 2:30 a.m. and had made no effort to re-drape it, because the booth was in what the nightshift considered a dead zone, a stretch of floor that even the rats passed through without pausing.

Bell picked up the wire. He re-draped it. He positioned the transmitter at the precise angle he had determined, through two weeks of experimentation, was most likely to catch the attention of a passerby — tilted eleven degrees forward, so that the brass cone of the mouthpiece seemed to be offering itself, conversationally, to anyone who glanced in its direction. He set the receiver on a small velvet pad. He placed, beside it, a handwritten card that read: "SPEAK INTO THE INSTRUMENT. YOUR VOICE WILL BE CARRIED BY ELECTRICAL CURRENT TO A RECEIVER AT THE OPPOSITE END OF THE WIRE. THE FUTURE OF HUMAN COMMUNICATION."

The card had been there since opening day. It had a coffee ring on it.

Bell straightened it. He waited.

The morning crowds streamed past. They streamed, specifically, toward the east nave, where the main attractions clustered — the Remington typewriting machine, the Otis elevator, a wallpaper-printing press that could produce twelve colors simultaneously and which, for reasons Bell could not fathom, drew a larger crowd than any electrical exhibit on the grounds. In the opposite direction, past Bell's booth, past the restrooms, and around a corner that required an active navigational decision, the foot traffic thinned to a trickle. Bell's booth was less a destination than a cul-de-sac.

By ten o'clock, three people had stopped. One was a child who wanted to know if the brass cone was a trumpet. One was a woman who had been looking for the restrooms and, upon being told they were "just past the partition, madam, to your left," had thanked Bell and left without glancing at the exhibit. The third was a man from the Centennial Guard — one of the security patrol — who stopped not out of curiosity about the telephone but because Bell's booth was adjacent to what the guard called his "eleven-o'clock post," a spot against the wall where, each day, he ate a hard-boiled egg and read the *Public Ledger* in peace.

"Still here?" the guard said, peeling his egg.

"Still here," said Bell.

"Judges come through today, I heard."

"This afternoon. Three o'clock."

The guard nodded. He did not ask what the judges were judging. In six weeks of proximity, he had never asked Bell to explain the telephone, and Bell had never volunteered, because he had learned — slowly, painfully, through dozens of failed attempts to engage the fair's workers in conversation about electromagnetic acoustics — that the people who kept the Centennial running did not want to hear about the future of human communication. They wanted to hear about booth-rental invoicing, lavatory maintenance schedules, and whether the oyster stand's new location violated the vendor-spacing ordinance.

"Oysters," the guard said, reading his paper.

"I'm sorry?"

"The oyster stand moved again. Did you see? They're practically in the entrance vestibule now. Pettit's going to lose his mind."

Bell had not seen. Bell did not know who Pettit was. Bell said, "Ah," which was his all-purpose response to workplace intelligence he did not possess, and returned to his transmitter, adjusting its angle by a degree he would not be able to measure and which would make no difference.

In the distance, at the center of Machinery Hall, the Corliss engine turned. Its walking beams rose and fell with the synchronized patience of a sleeping giant's breath. The belts turned. The shafts spun beneath the floor. The flywheel, fifty-six tons of cast iron rotating imperceptibly, held in its momentum enough energy to level the building, a fact that Hoskins, the chief engineer, liked to mention to visitors in the tone of a man discussing a large but well-trained dog.

Elsewhere on the grounds, the morning proceeded according to the logic of its labor. In Agricultural Hall, a woman named Josephine Strand was setting up the day's butter-sculpture display — today's subject was a sleeping baby, rendered in seventeen pounds of premium creamery butter — and arguing with a colleague about refrigeration allocations. The pneumatic tube system that connected the major halls was experiencing its daily 9 a.m. blockage, cause unknown, which the tube operators blamed on Agricultural Hall's habit of sending oversized message canisters and which Agricultural Hall blamed on the tube operators' failure to maintain adequate pressure. Outside the Main Building, on the plaza, in a display area that was technically under the jurisdiction of no hall and therefore no janitorial crew — a bureaucratic no-man's-land that Calloway found both infuriating and metaphysically satisfying — stood the right arm and torch of a statue that had not yet been finished, much less named. It was the future *Liberty Enlightening the World*, and it stood thirty-nine feet tall, the copper torch accessible by an interior ladder, and visitors could, for fifty cents, climb up inside the arm and stand on the balcony ringing the torch's flame and see the whole of the fairground spread out before them like a model of a world that had figured out what it was for.

The torch had its own crew: a ticket-taker, a guard who stood at the base, and a second guard who stood at the top to ensure no one leaned too far over the railing. The top guard was named Henshaw. Henshaw had the best view on the grounds and the worst knees, and he spent his shifts looking out across the Exposition and cataloging its problems with the comprehensive disapproval of a man who could see everything and fix nothing.

From the torch, the fair lay like a diagram of its own pretensions: the Main Building, the largest enclosed structure in the world, 1,880 feet long, its glass-and-iron roof glittering in the June sun; Machinery Hall beside it, venting steam; Agricultural Hall and Horticultural Hall and Memorial Hall and the Women's Pavilion and the forty-odd smaller buildings and pavilions and beer gardens spreading outward like a city that had been wished into existence and would be wished away by November.

Henshaw looked down. He could see the cream-puff line. He could see the oyster stand in its new, controversial location. He could see a young man with muttonchop whiskers standing alone at a booth near the back of the Main Building, adjusting something on a table, his posture suggesting he was waiting for someone who did not intend to come.

Henshaw did not know the man's name. Henshaw did not know that by five o'clock that afternoon, the man would be responsible for saving the lives of approximately three hundred hostages, would have caused more structural damage to the Exposition than any single person before or since, and would be standing in the wreckage of the Main Building's west transept holding a length of copper wire in one hand and a speaking trumpet in the other, bleeding from a cut above his left eye and shouting something into the trumpet that no one would be able to hear because his voice would be gone.

Henshaw saw none of this. He saw a man at a booth with no customers.

"Poor bastard," he said, to no one, because no one was at the top, because it was early and the fifty-cent climbers hadn't started yet.

Below, the fair hummed. The belts turned. The butter softened. The cream puffs sold. The vestibule remained unswept.

---

## II.

For the purposes of understanding what happened next, it is necessary to understand the telegraph, and to understand the telegraph it is necessary to understand what it meant to build one.

Not to invent one. Invention was a parlor trick — Samuel Morse in a room with wire and theory and the unearned confidence of a portrait painter who'd decided he was a scientist. Building a telegraph network was something else entirely. Building a telegraph network meant stringing copper wire from New York to San Francisco, which meant crossing the Allegheny Mountains, the Great Plains, the Rocky Mountains, the Sierra Nevada, and every river, gorge, box canyon, and ice storm in between. It meant cedar poles, fourteen thousand of them between Omaha and Sacramento alone, each one cut, stripped, hauled by mule team, planted in ground that was, depending on the season, frozen solid, flooded, or occupied by people who had reasonable objections to the project. narrative_idea_gen_taxonomy_profile.Super Genre: Action: Visceral stories featuring a resourceful hero against a single-minded villain, often involving intense physical conflict or chases.
narrative_idea_gen_taxonomy_profile.Macro/Micro Genre: Workplace: Views characters in a two-dimensional way, only seeing them at work. -> Boss’s Story/What It’s Like/Worker’s Story: The perspective of the workplace narrative.
narrative_idea_gen_taxonomy_profile.Voice: Metafiction and Faux-Nonfiction: Pseudo-Documentary (Historical Figure): Uses known historical figures to hook people into a fictional story.
narrative_idea_gen_taxonomy_profile.Pathway: Subverted Journeys (Road Trip/Journey): Protagonist embarks on a journey but does not return to their normal world.
narrative_idea_gen_taxonomy_profile.POV: Primary Omniscient: The story is viewed through the main character’s personal lens, but the narrative can take the reader anywhere.
